title: A hymn in Ramkali
hookLine: Ramkali holds the Anand, the Sadd, the Oankar and the Sidh Gosht: bliss, a farewell, an alphabet and a debate

lines: A CELEBRATION, A FAREWELL, A SCHOOL.
cards: One heading, Raga Ramkali, and under it, a song of bliss. A few pages on, a deathbed and a farewell. A few more, an alphabet poem that talks back to a teacher.
Then a long debate with yogis, seated in their circle. If a raga is a room, this one has guests from a celebration, a funeral, a schoolroom and a yogis' circle, all on the same carpet.
Today: a walk through that room, and one hymn to listen to.

teach.h: THE ANAND: BLISS HAS COME, MOTHER.
teach.b: First, the Anand, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, on ang nine seventeen. It opens, in paraphrase: bliss has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru.
Sikhs sing part of it at the close of gatherings, so the end of a service sounds like that first line. Second, the Sadd, a few pages on, a poem by Sundar.
It tells how Guru Amar Das, near his death, called his family together and told them not to weep for him. When I'm gone, he says in the poem, let the Lord's praises be heard instead.
And he places Ram Das as the next Guru.
A farewell that asks for songs, not tears.

Third, the Oankar, Guru Nanak's alphabet poem, beginning from Oankar, the One who brought forth creation. Its refrain speaks to a pandit, a teacher: listen, pandit, why write down the world's tangles?

teach.h: THE SIDH GOSHT: WHO ARE YOU?
teach.b: Fourth, the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's conversation with the Siddhas, the yogis. They open with blunt questions, in paraphrase: who are you, what's your name, what's your path, what are you after?
And the long answer comes back, again and again, to the Word and the Name.

So this path calls Ramkali the richest raga. Not because its music is better than the others, but because one heading holds a celebration, a farewell, a lesson and a debate, and every one ends up at the same place.

how: Sikhs sing part of the Anand Sahib, from Raga Ramkali, at the close of congregational gatherings, and the Sidh Gosht, the Oankar and the Sadd are read and sung from the same section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: what does “a hymn in ramkali” mean?
o: one raga holding the Anand, the Sadd, the Oankar and more
the raga of a farmer's aarti and a barber's lamp of ghee
a single poem the yogis sang to Guru Nanak in their circle

games.q: the guests in Ramkali — tap the pairs.
p: an alphabet pointed at the Name

s: in the Sadd, Guru Amar Das asks his family to mourn him with weeping
he tells them not to weep, and to sing the Lord's praises instead.
the Oankar speaks to a pandit, a teacher
its refrain: listen, pandit, why write down the world's tangles?
the Sidh Gosht opens with the Guru questioning the yogis
the yogis ask first: who are you, what's your name, what's your path?

games.q: you're Guru Amar Das, near the end. your family is gathered and some are starting to cry. what do you ask of them?
o: to mourn you for a long season.
not to weep, but to sing the Lord's praises.
games.why: in the Sadd, he tells them not to weep for him and asks for the Lord's praises to be sung, and he places Ram Das as the next Guru.

practice: If you can, play the opening of the Anand, often found as anand bhaiaa meree maae, and let it run; if not, take the yogis' first question slowly for yourself: who are you?
Don't answer with your job or your name; let the question sit, then let the Anand's first line answer it in its own way, bliss has come, with one Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Ramkali. One raga holding the Anand's bliss, the Sadd's farewell, the Oankar's alphabet and the Sidh Gosht's debate, all pointed at the Name. Today's word.

orig.note: anand, bliss, the name of Guru Amar Das's song in Ramkali.

carryVoice: Your line: the richest raga. Bliss, a farewell, a lesson and a debate, all ending at the Name. See you tomorrow.
